 Advertisement Florida's East Coast faces high flood risk after record rainfall
 Florida should be in its dry season, but yet another rainmaker this month had other plans.
 By Jonathan Belles and Jonathan Erdman • 1 hour ago Updated: November 20, 2026, 6:54 am EST Published: November 20, 2026, 7:30 am EST Share Share
 1 . Happening now Chevron Down Highest flood danger continues in parts of Florida on Friday
 Florida's Atlantic coast has been inundated with flooding rain for the second time in less than three weeks, smashing some November, fall and even all-time records near the state's Atlantic coast from Ft. Lauderdale to Melbourne. Now, they're under NOAA's highest risk category for flooding. 
 This is one more sign that El Niño is poised to bring a wet winter to the Sunshine State in what would typically be its dry season. 
 Happening now
 As the radar image below shows, bands of heavy rain continue to wrap into Florida's East Coast, primarily along the Space Coast and First Coast, including areas hit with flooding rain around the beginning of November.

 Parts of the Space Coast from north of Melbourne to Daytona Beach have picked up 10 to 20 inches of rain this week. 
 NOAA's Weather Prediction Center has issued their highest level of flash flood threats for parts of the Atlantic coast again Friday.

 The highest risk area includes Daytona Beach and Titusville. This is what NOAA said when they upgrade the risk to "high risk" on Thursday: 
 The rain may briefly include storms producing multiple-inch-per-hour rainfall rates, but it’s the fact that even with the lower rates, any and all rainfall in this area will have nowhere to go except to worsen already all-time-record breaking flooding. With the aforementioned impacts already occurring, the rainfall will continue to worsen them. Nearly half of these "high risk" days lead to at least one flood fatality or injury, according to NOAA.
 Day-by-day forecast
 Friday's heaviest rain will be along the Space and First Coasts of Florida as these heavy rainbands slowly lift northward. 
 This is some good news ahead. 
 As low pressure offshore organizes Saturday, that should put an end to the stationary bands of heavy rain near the coast. However, some locally heavy downpours are still possible across the Sunshine State Saturday. 
 By Sunday, much of the state should dry out, except only some lingering isolated bands of showers. 
 Forecast additional rainfall
 The heaviest additional rainfall through Saturday is expected to be on Florida's East Coast, between Cape Canaveral and the Florida-Georgia border. 
 At least 3 more inches is anticipated in this area, but some communities could see more than a foot of additional rain in the heaviest, most persistent rainbands.
 Those are the communities that are most likely to see additional flooding. 
 Records have been obliterated
 The combination of this latest heavy rain event, one around the beginning of November, and a generally wet stretch of the fall, has smashed monthly, seasonal and even river crest records in the eastern Florida Peninsula. 
 Melbourne's rainfall is most off the charts. 
 Wettest single month dating to 1937 (22.59 inches through Nov. 19)
 Almost 13 inches wetter than their previous wettest November in 1963 (9.72 inches), all in just 19 days
 Wettest autumn (Sept. through Nov.), with 42.54 inches
 Nov. 2 was their record wettest single day (11.51 inches)
 Ft. Lauderdale (15.49 inches), Vero Beach (12.32 inches) and West Palm Beach (18.25 inches) also smashed their record wettest November. 
 And west of Cocoa Beach, the slowly oozing St. Johns River , still in major flood following the early November deluge, topped its record flood from October 1953, swamping neighborhoods. 
 Why is it so wet this year? 
 October always brings a breath of fresh air to Floridians, but this year it might be the only drier skies we might see for a while. 
 Crack open your favorite beverage: We're going to be talking about El Niño again. 
 The dry season across the Florida peninsula is supposed to be from October through May, but this year El Niño is likely to bring rainfall amounts that are more akin to the middle of thunderstorm season.
 That's because El Niño amplifies a jet stream across the subtropics and over Florida during the winter months. This acts like train tracks for storm systems to come from the Pacific, across the Southern U.S. and into Florida. 
 Worse than just rain, the winter months during an El Niño can also bring several rounds of severe weather, including tornadoes. 
 That same jet stream that brings rain also brings an abundant supply of one of the ingredients needed for severe weather: wind shear . Wind shear is the change of winds in direction and/or strength with height. This changing of winds can cause the atmosphere to roll and twist, leading to tornadoes.
